figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: ReCache preserves text and visual fidelity under high acceleration on FLUX.1-dev Black Forest Labs (2024). Under a $5.4\times$ acceleration, heuristic baselines (TaylorSeer Liu et al. (2025b), DPCache Cui et al. (2026)) fail to maintain image quality and corrupt text spelling. By framing scheduling as an RL problem, ReCache allocates computations to the most critical steps, closely matching Full inference at the same computational cost.
figures.headline: At 5.4 times acceleration on FLUX.1-dev, TaylorSeer and DPCache corrupt text spelling while ReCache stays close to full inference.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 1, for a fixed computational budget, our learned policy produces outputs that more closely match the full-inference generations than those from uniform or heuristic-adaptive baselines.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of the ReCache method. Given a target computational budget $k$, a lightweight MLP policy network predicts importance logits to perform a top-$k$ selection of inference steps for full computation. During the inference with caching, the selected steps are fully computed (green blocks), while the intermediate steps reuse or forecast features (red blocks). The policy is trained using the REINFORCE algorithm without backpropagating through the diffusion process. The reward formulation balances a Fidelity term (minimizing the distance to the $\mathbf{x}_{\text{full}}$ output from the full inference) and a Quality term (maximizing the perceptual quality of the generated $\mathbf{x}_{\text{cache}}$).
figures.headline: The policy selects k steps for full computation, and the remaining steps reuse or forecast features during inference.
citing_sentences: We introduce ReCache, a framework that trains a schedule policy: given a target budget $k$, the policy selects $k$ inference steps to recompute (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Impact of the quality reward coefficient $\alpha_{\text{iq}}$. Increasing $\alpha_{iq}$ improves HPS but worsens LPIPS, revealing a quality–fidelity trade-off. Optimizing only for HPS causes both metrics to collapse, highlighting the need for the LPIPS fidelity term. We use $\alpha_{iq}=7$ as the best trade-off.
figures.headline: Raising the quality reward weight improves HPS but worsens LPIPS, and optimizing HPS alone collapses both metrics.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 reports the effect of varying the coefficient $\alpha_{\text{iq}}$, which controls the relative strength of the latter.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison on FLUX.1-dev. Under strict compute budgets, the best heuristic baseline schedules (uniform, DiCache, DPCache) fail to maintain image fidelity, corrupting text spelling (top row), object composition (middle row), and fine-grained details (bottom row). By learning an optimal budget-aware schedule, ReCache successfully preserves these critical visual structures at the exact same computational cost.
figures.headline: Under strict budgets on FLUX.1-dev, heuristic schedules corrupt text, layouts and fine details where ReCache preserves them.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 shows that heuristic schedules can fail under aggressive caching, producing corrupted text, distorted object layouts, and missing fine-grained details.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison on Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo for the prompt "a zebra bending down to drink water from a river". Under tight computational budgets, baseline scheduling strategies produce visible artifacts such as color degradation and structural blurring, while ReCache, using the same caching mechanism and budget, restores quality and more closely matches full inference.
figures.headline: Under tight budgets, baseline schedules on Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo show color degradation and blur that ReCache avoids.
citing_sentences: The same pattern extends to video generation, as shown in Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Comparison of cache steps for FLUX.1-dev with the caching mechanisms TaylorSeer ($O=2$) and Taylor-DP ($O=2$)
figures.headline: Cache steps chosen by the budget-aware policy on FLUX.1-dev are plotted across target budgets for two second-order caching mechanisms.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 plots the specific cache steps assigned by our budget-aware policy across different target budgets.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Effect of the entropy regularization coefficient $\lambda_{\text{entropy}}$ on ReCache. Increasing entropy encourages the discovery of more optimal schedules and is particularly beneficial under looser budget constraints; however, excessively high values can slow convergence.
figures.headline: Raising the entropy coefficient helps most at looser budgets, while excessively high values slow convergence.

abstract: Modern diffusion models generate high-quality images and videos, but their iterative denoising process makes inference expensive. Feature caching accelerates sampling by reusing or predicting intermediate activations across neighboring denoising steps, exploiting the redundancy of computations along the reverse trajectory. In this work, we focus on the caching schedule: selecting which denoising steps should be fully recomputed. Existing schedules are either fixed (e.g. uniform) or chosen adaptively from per-step error heuristics; in both cases, the actual compute cost is a side-effect of hand-tuned thresholds rather than a quantity the user can specify. We propose ReCache, which inverts this: given a target budget $k$, it learns the recomputation schedule that maximizes generation quality, turning compute into a directly controllable input. ReCache trains via policy gradients, sidestepping backpropagation through full diffusion inference, and uses no labelled data. Generations from uncached inference serve as matching targets, paired with a reward for generation quality. ReCache is compatible with any caching mechanism, including feature reuse and feature forecasting; for each mechanism, a single trained policy adapts across computational budgets at inference time. ReCache consistently outperforms scheduling baselines: under a $\times 5.04$ FLOPs reduction on FLUX, it reduces LPIPS by 31% (from 0.456 to 0.316) compared to DiCache; on Wan 2.1 at a $\sim\times 2.6$ speedup, it drops LPIPS by 65% (from 0.480 to 0.169) and boosts the VBench score by 7% (5.6 points, from 70.4 to 76.0) over uniform HiCache. Code is available at https://github.com/thecrazymage/ReCache.

sections.body: Diffusion inference is costly because each sampling step runs a large network, and feature caching reuses activations across steps. Most caching methods pick which steps to recompute with hand-crafted rules. ReCache instead treats the caching schedule as a learned policy trained with reinforcement learning. Given a target budget, it predicts which steps need full computation, optimizing output consistency with the full-inference result. The authors evaluate it on FLUX.1-dev, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, combined with TaylorSeer and HiCache, and report consistent gains over hand-crafted schedules at equal cost.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Hand-crafted caching schedules are replaced by a learned, budget-aware policy trained with reinforcement learning.

sections.body: A diffusion model runs N inference steps, and each step evaluates a diffusion transformer, which dominates the per-step cost. A caching schedule is a subset of cache steps, where the network runs in full. Its size k is the caching budget, which sets the number of full model evaluations. Reuse steps rebuild missing activations from the cache. Direct reuse mechanisms copy the most recent cached activations, as in FORA and Δ-DiT. Forecasting mechanisms extrapolate from several earlier cached steps: TaylorSeer fits a Taylor polynomial, and HiCache uses a basis better suited to diffusion feature trajectories. ReCache is agnostic to which mechanism is used.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Caching splits denoising steps into fully computed steps and reuse steps, with mechanisms that either reuse or forecast features.

sections.body: ReCache parameterizes the schedule as a Plackett-Luce distribution over k-subsets of denoising steps. A lightweight MLP maps the budget k to importance logits, and the top-k steps form the schedule. The training loss combines a patch-wise LPIPS distance between cached and full-inference outputs with an HPSv2 reward subtracted with a weight. An entropy bonus keeps the policy exploring. Gradients come from leave-one-out policy-gradient estimates, so the diffusion process is never backpropagated through. Each training sample pairs a prompt and an initial noise with its full-inference output, and budgets are sampled during training.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A budget-conditioned policy over step subsets is trained with policy gradients to balance fidelity and reward.

sections.body: Experiments use FLUX.1-dev for images, with 50 steps at 1024×1024, and HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video. Budgets of 7, 9 and 13 full-computation steps are tested. Image evaluation uses 1000 MS-COCO prompts with LPIPS and HPSv2, plus ImageReward on 200 DrawBench prompts. Video evaluation uses frame-level LPIPS and HPSv2 on 110 VBench prompts, plus the VBench score over 944 prompts. Within every mechanism and budget cell, ReCache improves LPIPS and the perceptual metrics over the hand-designed schedule. Gains are largest at the tightest budget, k=7, where ReCache often closes most of the gap to full inference. Ablations show the budget-aware predictor stays within 0.001 of per-budget specialists on HPS while improving LPIPS at every budget.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: ReCache outperforms hand-designed schedules on LPIPS and perceptual reward across FLUX.1-dev, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1.

sections.body: The conclusion states that ReCache finds schedules with superior quality compared with modern baselines on FLUX.1-dev, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1. The stated limitation is that all feature caching methods, including this one, give limited benefits in low-step regimes of one to four steps, where large gaps between reuse points make cached features less informative. The broader impacts note that faster sampling also lowers the cost of misuse. The method changes only the sampling procedure, so it inherits the filtering, watermarking, or access controls of the underlying model. The authors recommend pairing it with provenance tooling.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: ReCache gives limited benefit in one-to-four-step regimes and inherits the safety properties of the underlying model.

sections.body: Appendix A surveys diffusion acceleration and caching, including what-to-cache, how-to-use, and adaptive when-to-cache methods, and places ReCache as a learned policy. Appendix B describes the modified MS-COCO prompt set, baseline implementations, and training settings for FLUX.1-dev, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, including a policy MLP of approximately 100K parameters. Appendix C reports extended FLUX.1-dev text-to-image results and ablations. Appendix D reports training cost in GPU hours on H100 hardware. Figures in the appendix plot cache steps and the effect of the entropy coefficient.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, implementation details for baselines and models, extended FLUX results, compute cost, and figures.
